1.pericope_label: The king shall joy in thy strength: thanks for a prayer answered, a crown of gold and length of days

schools.summary: Gill reads every clause of the King Messiah, the strength communicated to his human nature and the blessings put into his hands before he was manifest in the flesh; Calvin keeps the thanksgiving David’s while holding the Spirit’s design was to direct the faithful to Christ, the end and perfection of this kingdom.

Henry has the people congratulate their king and turn his answered prayer into their own praise, no prayer being accepted but what is the heart’s desire; Spurgeon begins from Jesus as a royal personage, King over minds and hearts, proclaimed so even on the cross.

Clarke prefers David’s Ammonite victory as the occasion, takes the preventing back to its Latin sense of going before, and reads the fourth verse of the Messiah of whom David was the type; Wesley glosses the blessings as more and sooner than expected and the countenance as a smile of grace.

Ellicott renders the opening as a present, traces the unique word for request to a root meaning to be poor, and refuses to let an allusion to the eternal kingdom be forced on the text; Delitzsch reports the Targum and Talmud for the king Messiah and Rashi’s wish to abandon that reading, and settles for David whose cause is figuratively that of Christ.

debates: Whom is the psalm about? Clarke canvasses the occasions and prefers David’s victory over the Ammonites to the guesses of Sennacherib or Hezekiah; Delitzsch reports the Targum and the Talmud for the king Messiah and Rashi’s remark that the Messianic reading ought to be given up for the Christians’ sake, then settles for David as figuratively Christ; Calvin and Henry keep David in front with an eye to Christ; Spurgeon and Gill read it of Christ throughout; Ellicott refuses the move entirely, holding that an allusion to the eternal kingdom is not to be forced on the passage and that for ever and ever is merely a term for indefinite length.

What is the crown of the third verse? Clarke and Delitzsch both make it the Ammonite diadem of Rabbah, Delitzsch adding that the verse cannot mean a first coronation but the increase of a kingship’s honour; Ellicott lists Rabbah, a coronation and Ewald’s birthday celebration and settles for a symbol of victory, maidens being accustomed to meet a monarch returning in triumph with a garland.

Was the request made in sickness or after a victory? Ellicott finds the evidence pulling both ways, the prayer for length of life suggesting sickness while the psalm’s tone suggests victory, and leaves it open; Clarke reports the sickness reading as the ground on which some refer the whole psalm to Hezekiah, and declines it.
outliers: Clarke alone illustrates the older English sense of prevent from a royal speech before Agincourt, beside the collect that asks God to prevent us in all our doings.
Delitzsch alone records that Rashi thought the Messianic interpretation of this psalm ought rather to be given up for the sake of the Christians.
Calvin alone makes the point that David could have thanked God privately but meant to testify that his blessings redounded to the public good of all the faithful.
Delitzsch alone compares the sixth verse with the word to Abram, a blessing both possessed and passed on.
themes: a psalm paired with the one before it
whether the king is David or the Messiah
a word for request found nowhere else
blessings that arrive before they are asked
a crown taken from a conquered city
length of days as an indefinite term

7.pericope_label: For the king trusteth in the Lord: a throne unmoved, and enemies found out and consumed

schools.summary: Gill names the Targum’s King Messiah as the one who trusts, unrolls a long roll of who the enemies are from the Jews and Gentiles to the followers of the man of sin and the devil, and grounds the finding on omniscience and the holding on omnipotence.

Henry makes the seventh verse the ground of the people’s courage as the first was the ground of their thanks, and hears the enemies’ designs aimed higher than the throne, since those who would unking David would in effect un-God Jehovah; Spurgeon takes the trusting king for a master in the use of the weapons and calls a holy confidence in Jehovah the true mother of victories.

Clarke disclaims skill and valour for faith in a conquering arm, has an uncontrollable power reach the enemies wherever hidden, and makes one class of sinners the means of consuming another; Wesley says only that they go like wood cast in, and takes the fruit for children.

Ellicott marks the turn from addressing Jehovah to addressing the king, calls the oven figure most obscure and mends it by a very slight change, and traces the withering face back to Jehovah in the next clause; Delitzsch marks the same structural turn and grounds the oven in the fate of Rabbath Ammon.

debates: Where does the psalm turn? Ellicott notes that it has until now addressed Jehovah and here turns in prophetic strain to the king; Delitzsch marks the same place as the opening of the second half and insists the change carries confident expectation rather than wish.

What is the fiery oven? Ellicott calls the figure most obscure as it stands and gets the sense by a very slight change to thou shalt put them into a fiery oven, taking the image from a smelter’s furnace rather than from Sodom; Gill reports both the brick-kiln and the Sodom guesses and prefers the same change; Delitzsch grounds it in history, the arrival of David having decided the fall of Rabbath Ammon, whose people were cast into brick-kilns.

Whose face withers the wicked? Ellicott takes the time of thine anger literally as of thy face, observes that a power usually ascribed to the face of God is here given to his representative, and has the poet refer it back to Jehovah in the next clause; Delitzsch reads the face the same way, as the personal appearing of the king.
outliers: Spurgeon alone remarks that the psalm of triumph was composed long before the conflict, faith overleaping time to chant her triumph while still singing her battle song.
Gill alone names the enemies individually, from the Jews who would not have him reign to the Roman emperors, the followers of the man of sin, and professors who oppose him in practice.
Henry alone presses the designs back to their object, that those who aimed to unking David aimed in effect to un-God Jehovah.
themes: a verse that turns from God to the king
confidence as the mother of victories
an oven mended by one letter
a face that withers with a glance
evil intended and no power to perform it

12.pericope_label: Therefore shalt thou make them turn their back: the arrows aimed, and a closing call to be exalted

schools.summary: Gill offers three senses of the turned back, flight to hiding places from the wrath of God and of the Lamb, God turning his own back and disregarding their cry, or the Targum’s separation of them to one side; and he finds the closing exertion of strength fulfilled at the fall of Jerusalem, again at the fall of Babylon, and finally at the day of judgment.

Clarke reads the turning as panic, since God can strike the most numerous army in its moment of victory, turns the closing imperative round because creatures cannot exalt their maker, and asks which attribute is to be praised, answering that each man celebrates the perfection most shown in his own deliverance; Wesley says only that it is by his own power, or the manifestation of it.

Ellicott gives the Hebrew of the twelfth verse literally as thou shalt put them shoulder and prefers the English version to the alternative rendering, and notes that the last verse turns back to address Jehovah; Delitzsch calls making them into a back a more choice expression than the usual idiom, and hears the whole psalm close by soaring aloft and losing itself in a distich.

debates: What does it mean to make them turn their back? Ellicott gives the Hebrew literally as thou shalt put them shoulder, quoting the Vulgate, and prefers the English version to the rendering shalt strike them back; Delitzsch calls making them into such as turn the back to you a more choice expression than the usual idiom; Gill offers flight, or God turning his own back on them, or the Targum’s reading that they are set together on one side and separated from the people of God; Clarke reads a panic that makes them turn as though a volley of arrows had been discharged in their faces.

What is asked by be thou exalted? Delitzsch makes it a cry for victory in battle on the king’s behalf, God manifesting himself in his supernal and judicial sovereignty, with a joyous gratitude promised in advance; Clarke turns it round, exalt thyself, for thy creatures cannot exalt thee; Gill reads it as an exertion of strength fulfilled at three successive judgments; Wesley reduces it to the manifestation of his own power.
outliers: Clarke alone distributes the duty of praise by attribute, so that one who is taught celebrates wisdom, one who is strengthened magnifies power, and one who is saved makes mercy the burden of his song.
Clarke alone quotes the old Anglo-Scottish Psalter, that we shall make known his words in good will and good work, for he sings well that works well.
Delitzsch alone describes the form of the whole psalm, twice three tetrastichs closing in a distich.
Clarke alone observes that God can give victory to his people over the most formidable enemies though they strike not one blow in their own defence.
themes: a shoulder turned instead of a back
a song that closes in a distich
a creature that cannot exalt its maker
praise matched to the attribute shown
